mri-scan-what-to-expect.name: MRI scan: what to expect and what it shows
mri-scan-what-to-expect.summary: An MRI scan uses a strong magnet and radio waves, not X-rays, to take detailed pictures. This guide covers noise, safety checks, contrast and results.
keyPoints: MRI uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to take detailed pictures, and it does not use X-rays.
The scanner is loud, so earplugs or headphones are provided, and staff can talk to the person through an intercom.
A safety questionnaire is completed first because some implanted devices can stop a scan from going ahead.
Results are not usually given on the day: a radiologist reports the images to the doctor who requested the scan.

body.heading: What is an MRI scan?
body.body:
MRI uses a strong magnet and radio waves to build images of the inside of the body. It does not use X-rays or other ionising radiation. The person operating the scanner watches from another room.

Scan length depends on the area examined, and NHS trust leaflets quote different times, from about 10 minutes to about 90 minutes. One trust says the total time in the department is likely to be about an hour.

body.heading: What happens during the scan?
body.body:
Staff settle the person on a couch that slides into the scanner. An intercom lets the person talk to the radiographer during the scan. The person is asked to keep still, because movement can blur the pictures.

Some scans include an injection of contrast, a dye that helps to produce a more detailed picture and improves the accuracy of the scan. Some scans use contrast dye, which NHS trust leaflets say is injected into a vein through a small tube called a cannula. NHS Inform says complications are rare, but some people have side effects or an allergic reaction to the contrast dye.

body.heading: Why is the scanner so loud, and what if it feels enclosed?
body.body: The scanner makes loud beeping or hammering noises, so earplugs or headphones are provided and some departments play music. The NHS says an MRI scan is noisy and may create a feeling of claustrophobia, which means feeling anxious in enclosed spaces. A study found that a wide-bore scanner increased the success rate of MRI in people with claustrophobia. A person who has a sedative needs someone to take them home afterwards.

body.heading: Is an MRI scan safe, and why is metal a concern?
body.body:
Before the scan each person completes a safety questionnaire. The NHS describes MRI as painless and safe, although it is noisy. The NHS says the MRI magnet is strong, so people with a metal implant such as a pacemaker or artificial joint may not be able to have a scan. The magnet is strong enough to pull strongly on some metals. NHS trust leaflets say patients are asked to remove magnetic objects and may change into a gown before the scan.

NHS safety policies say some implants, such as aneurysm clips and programmable shunt valves, can be scanned only if specific conditions are met. Some implants, including some pacemakers, are labelled MR conditional, which means they can be scanned only under set conditions. Trust leaflets ask people to tell the imaging staff about any implants.

body.heading: Do I need to prepare?
body.body: Most MRI scans need no special preparation, according to NHS trust information. Some scans of the abdomen or pelvis may need fasting for a few hours, and bowel-relaxing medicine is sometimes given.

body.heading: When do the results arrive?
body.body: Results are not usually given on the day of the scan. A radiologist, a doctor who specialises in reading scans, studies the images and writes a report for the doctor who requested the scan. That doctor then discusses the findings with the person. The NHS says complications from an MRI scan are rare, but some people get side effects or an allergic reaction to the contrast dye. Reactions to contrast dye usually happen soon after the injection, so some trusts ask people to stay for about 30 minutes afterwards.

references.title: King's College Hospital (NHS trust page): mri
Chelsea and Westminster (NHS trust page): mri

ct-scan-what-to-expect.name: CT scan: what happens, contrast and radiation
ct-scan-what-to-expect.summary: A CT scan uses X-rays and a computer to build slice pictures of the body. This guide covers preparation, contrast dye, radiation and when results arrive.
keyPoints: A CT scanner rotates an X-ray source around the body, and a computer builds cross-sectional slices that can be stacked into a three-dimensional picture.
CT uses more radiation than a standard X-ray, and MedlinePlus says the cancer risk from any one scan is small.
Some scans use an injected iodine-based dye called contrast, which can cause a warm flush and a metallic taste that usually pass quickly.
A radiologist reviews the images and sends a report to the doctor who requested the scan, who then discusses it with the person.

body.heading: What is a CT scan?
body.body: CT stands for computed tomography. A CT scanner rotates an X-ray source around the body while the person lies on a bed that moves through a ring shaped like a doughnut. Detectors on the opposite side pick up the X-rays, and a computer turns each rotation into a thin cross-sectional slice. The slices can be stacked to make a three-dimensional image. The NHS lists CT scans among the tests that use X-rays to give more detailed images than a standard X-ray.

body.heading: How do people prepare for a CT scan?
body.body: Instructions differ between hospitals, and the appointment letter has the local details. Instructions about eating and drinking before a CT scan differ between NHS trusts, and the appointment letter says which apply. Some scans of the abdomen or pelvis involve drinking extra fluid or a drink containing contrast beforehand. Some people have a blood test first, mainly to check how well the kidneys are working. NHS trust leaflets ask people to attend in loose clothing with anything metallic removed. Staff ask about allergies, especially to iodine or to earlier contrast dye, and about medicines the person takes.

body.heading: What happens during the scan?
body.body: The person lies on a flat, motorised table that slides into the scanner. They are asked to keep very still and may be asked to hold their breath for a few seconds. Leaflets quote different lengths for the scan itself, which is short, and the whole visit takes longer, especially when drinks are needed beforehand. After the scan the radiographer may ask the person to wait briefly while they check that no more images are needed, and the person is then free to leave.

body.heading: What is the contrast dye?
body.body:
Contrast is a substance that makes blood vessels, organs or other tissues easier to see. Depending on the area, it may be given by mouth, through a vein, or by enema. MedlinePlus says the most common type of contrast given into a vein contains iodine. MedlinePlus says contrast given through a vein can cause a slight burning feeling, a metallic taste and warm flushing, which usually fade quickly.

MedlinePlus says allergic reactions to the dye can happen, and that a life-threatening reaction is rare. MedlinePlus says contrast given through a vein can worsen kidney function, and that people with kidney disease or diabetes may be given extra fluids afterwards.

body.heading: How much radiation does a CT scan use?
body.body: A CT scan uses more radiation than an ordinary X-ray, and MedlinePlus says most new scanners can reduce the dose. MedlinePlus says having many X-rays or CT scans over time may raise the risk of cancer, but the risk from any one scan is small. An NHS trust leaflet says children are more sensitive to radiation and that a CT is done only when it is essential for making a diagnosis. Trust leaflets ask people who might be pregnant to tell the imaging team before the scan. The NHS says the cancer risk from X-ray tests is thought to be very small. GOV.UK safety advice says that when imaging is properly justified and optimised, the risks are much less than the risks of the conditions being investigated, and that cancers linked to radiation can take decades to develop. An NHS trust leaflet says the benefit of a test should be greater than its radiation risk.

body.heading: When do the results arrive?
body.body: A radiologist reviews the images and sends a report to the doctor who asked for the scan. That doctor then discusses the results with the person. Timing varies by hospital, and leaflets quote from about one or two weeks to about four weeks. Results are not given on the day.

x-ray-what-to-expect.name: X-ray: what to expect, safety and results
x-ray-what-to-expect.summary: An X-ray uses a small beam of radiation to picture bones, lungs and other parts. This guide covers the test, radiation risk, pregnancy and results.
keyPoints: An X-ray can produce images of many parts of the body, and the NHS lists fractures, teeth, lungs and the digestive system among them.
The NHS says a standard X-ray leaves no after-effects and the cancer risk is thought to be very small.
Trust leaflets say X-rays during pregnancy do not raise the risk of miscarriage, and that X-rays of the tummy or near the womb need special care.
The NHS says results may be given on the same day or at an appointment a few weeks later.

body.heading: What is an X-ray used for?
body.body: An X-ray uses a beam of electromagnetic radiation to make an image of the inside of the body. According to the NHS, X-rays can produce images of many parts of the body, including bones, teeth, lungs and the digestive system. They are used, for example, to check for broken bones after an accident.

body.heading: What happens during an X-ray?
body.body: The health professional who takes X-rays in hospital is called a radiographer. The radiographer positions the person sitting, lying or standing, depending on the part of the body. The X-ray itself takes only a few minutes, according to the NHS. The NHS says people are asked to remove metal items such as jewellery and zips. Some types need fasting for several hours beforehand.

body.heading: Which other tests use X-rays?
body.body: The NHS lists several related tests, including angiography, which checks blood vessels using a dye injected into the blood. It also lists DEXA scans, which measure bone density, and CT scans, which give more detailed images. Studies of the digestive system use a barium drink or enema, a liquid that shows up on X-ray.

body.heading: How much radiation is involved?
body.body: The NHS says a standard X-ray leaves no after-effects and the cancer risk is thought to be very small. The NHS says the risk of cancer from X-rays is thought to be very small. Trust leaflets say staff keep doses as low as possible and that a test goes ahead only when its benefit outweighs the small risk. GOV.UK safety advice says that when imaging is properly justified and optimised, the risks from X-ray examinations are far smaller than the risks of the conditions being investigated. GOV.UK safety advice says cancers linked to radiation can take decades to appear. The same advice says children have a higher lifetime risk from X-rays than adults, and that risk is lower for older patients because cancers take a long time to develop.

body.heading: Are X-rays safe in pregnancy?
body.body: Trusts ask anyone who might be pregnant to tell the team before an X-ray. NHS trust leaflets say X-rays during pregnancy do not raise the risk of miscarriage and, at typical doses, do not cause birth defects. The main concern it names is a very small increase in the chance that the baby develops cancer in childhood. Trust leaflets say X-rays of the tummy or near the womb need special care during pregnancy. A trust leaflet says X-rays of parts of the body away from the tummy, such as the head, chest, arms or lower legs, are fine to have during pregnancy. A test may go ahead during pregnancy if the health benefit clearly outweighs the small radiation risk to the baby.

body.heading: How and when do results come back?
body.body: A reporting radiographer or a radiologist, a doctor who specialises in imaging, reviews the X-ray. The report goes to the team that requested the test. The NHS says results may come on the same day or at an appointment a few weeks later, and that a clinician should explain them. Trusts quote different waits for the report, so timings differ between hospitals.

Gloucestershire Hospitals (NHS trust page): xray preg
Leicester's Hospitals (NHS trust page): xray preg

ultrasound-scan-what-to-expect.name: Ultrasound scan: what happens and is it safe
ultrasound-scan-what-to-expect.summary: An ultrasound scan uses sound waves, not radiation, to make live pictures. This guide covers the gel, the full bladder, internal scans and results.
keyPoints: An ultrasound scan uses sound waves rather than radiation, and the NHS describes the sound waves used as safe.
A water-based gel goes on the skin, and a small probe is moved over the area being scanned.
Pelvic and bladder scans usually need a full bladder, and the hospital or clinic explains how to prepare.
Some people have an internal (transvaginal) scan.

body.heading: What is an ultrasound scan?
body.body: An ultrasound scan uses high-frequency sound waves to make a picture of the inside of the body. The sound waves bounce off different parts of the body, and the echoes are picked up by a probe and turned into a moving image. It does not use radiation or X-rays. NHS and NHS trust pages describe ultrasound being used to look inside the body, to guide procedures such as biopsy and drainage, and during pregnancy. It can also help to guide a biopsy or the draining of fluid.

body.heading: What happens during the scan?
body.body: Gel is put on the skin over the area and a small probe is moved across it. The gel is water-based and washes off easily, and trust leaflets say it will not stain clothing. The NHS says an ultrasound scan takes around 10 to 45 minutes, and may take longer. Afterwards the gel can be wiped off and the person can get dressed.

body.heading: Why do some scans need a full bladder?
body.body: For pelvic and bladder scans, people are usually asked to arrive with a full bladder. Trust leaflets explain that a full bladder gives a clearer picture because sound waves travel more easily through fluid. Leaflets ask people not to empty their bladder until after the scan, and say a toilet is nearby afterwards. Scans of some organs, such as the liver, may need no food for several hours beforehand. The hospital or clinic tells people how to prepare for their type of scan.

body.heading: What are the different kinds of ultrasound scan?
body.body: The usual scan is external, with the probe on the skin. Some people have a transvaginal (internal) scan. For this scan the probe is disinfected, covered with a protective sheath and lubricated with gel. People usually need to empty their bladder first for an internal scan. Ultrasound can also be used to look at blood flow and at whether blood vessels are narrowed or blocked.

body.heading: Is an ultrasound scan safe?
body.body: The NHS says the sound waves used in ultrasound scans are safe, and that ultrasound scans do not use radiation. An NHS maternity leaflet says scans are painless and have no known side effects. One hospital notes that standard ultrasound gel is not sterile, so there is a very small risk of infection in some circumstances. People with a latex allergy are asked to tell the department beforehand so latex-free products can be used.

body.heading: When are the results shared?
body.body: The images are reviewed by the specialist who carried out the scan. The report goes to the doctor or team who requested the scan. The NHS says results may be given at the end of the appointment, or can take a few weeks, depending on the reason for the scan.

references.title: University Hospitals Birmingham (NHS trust page): us
North Tees and Hartlepool (NHS trust page): pelv us

ecg-what-it-records-and-shows.name: ECG: what it records and what it can show
ecg-what-it-records-and-shows.summary: An ECG records the heart's electrical activity through patches on the skin. This guide covers the test, longer recordings, what it shows and its limits.
keyPoints: An ECG records the electrical activity of the heart, including its rate and rhythm.
A standard ECG is quick and painless, and patches called electrodes are placed on the arms, legs and chest.
A standard ECG can miss an abnormal rhythm that is not happening during the recording, which is why longer monitoring is sometimes used.
An ECG can help doctors tell whether someone is having a heart attack or has had one in the past.

body.heading: What does an ECG record?
body.body: An electrocardiogram, or ECG, records the electrical activity of the heart. The British Heart Foundation describes it as a simple test that records the heart's rhythm, its rate and its electrical activity. Each heartbeat is triggered by an electrical signal, and the machine picks these signals up through sensors on the skin. The result is a graph of the signals.

body.heading: What happens during a standard ECG?
body.body: Sticky patches called electrodes are placed on the arms, legs and chest and connected to the machine. The British Heart Foundation describes the test as quick and painless. The NHS puts a standard ECG at about 5 minutes. People are asked to lie still because movement can affect the recording.

body.heading: What can an ECG show?
body.body: The British Heart Foundation says an ECG can help doctors to tell whether someone is having a heart attack or has had one in the past. The NHS says an ECG is usually done when a doctor suspects symptoms of a heart attack, coronary heart disease or an abnormal heart rhythm (arrhythmia).

body.heading: What are the limits of a standard ECG?
body.body: A standard ECG captures only what happens while it is recording. A standard ECG can miss an abnormal rhythm that is not happening during the recording. That is why longer recordings or other heart tests are sometimes arranged.

body.heading: What are longer and exercise ECGs?
body.body: An ambulatory ECG, sometimes called Holter monitoring, records the heart's electrical activity continuously while the person goes about daily life. The NHS says people are usually asked to wear it for 24 to 48 hours, but it can be up to 7 days. It is used to look for heart rhythm problems that a short recording may miss. An exercise ECG monitors the heart while the person exercises and the heart is working harder. The British Heart Foundation describes an exercise ECG as an ECG recorded while the person walks on a treadmill or cycles, used to see how the heart behaves under exertion and to look for coronary heart disease. Doctors may suggest it for symptoms such as dizzy spells or blackouts. It is also used after procedures such as angioplasty, and to help set exercise levels for cardiac rehabilitation. The person walks or cycles at a gentle pace that gradually gets harder, and staff watch closely.

body.heading: How do the results reach the person?
body.body: The NHS says people may need a follow-up appointment to talk about their ECG results. The NHS says ECG results may be available on the same day, but can take a few weeks depending on the type of ECG. The British Heart Foundation says to call 999 immediately for signs of a heart attack, such as sudden chest pain that does not ease after a few minutes of rest.

references.title: University Hospitals Sussex (NHS trust page): ecg
Sandwell and West Birmingham (NHS trust page): ecg
Sandwell and West Birmingham (NHS trust page): amb

echocardiogram-types-and-what-it-shows.name: Echocardiogram: types, what happens and results
echocardiogram-types-and-what-it-shows.summary: An echocardiogram uses ultrasound to picture the heart. This guide explains the standard, stress and throat versions and what each involves.
keyPoints: The most common type is a transthoracic echocardiogram, in which a probe is placed over the chest.
A stress echocardiogram is done during exercise or after a medicine that has a similar effect on the heart.
A transoesophageal echocardiogram passes a probe down the throat and gives more detailed pictures than the standard test.
Most people need no preparation for a standard echocardiogram, but may need to avoid eating for several hours before the throat version.

body.heading: What is an echocardiogram?
body.body: An echocardiogram is a scan that uses ultrasound, high-frequency sound waves, to produce moving pictures of the heart. An ultrasound probe covered in gel is placed on the chest in the standard test.

body.heading: What are the types of echocardiogram?
body.body: The most common type is the transthoracic echocardiogram, in which the probe is placed over the chest. A transoesophageal echocardiogram uses a probe that passes down the throat and gives more detailed pictures of the heart than the standard test. Doctors may use it when the standard test has not shown enough detail. A stress echocardiogram is a transthoracic scan done during exercise on a treadmill or exercise bike, or after a medicine that has a similar effect on the heart. For some echocardiograms, saline or a special dye is injected into a vein to help show the heart more clearly. A stress echocardiogram may be recommended if a heart problem is triggered by physical activity.

body.heading: What happens in the throat version?
body.body: For the transoesophageal test, the back of the throat is numbed with an anaesthetic spray. A sedative may be given to help the person relax. Avoiding food for several hours beforehand may be needed for this version. Afterwards the throat may be sore, and this should pass within one or two days.

body.heading: What can an echocardiogram show?
body.body: An NHS trust says a transoesophageal echocardiogram can look at the heart valves and heart muscle, and check for blood clots and tears in the aorta. An NHS trust says it can help guide surgeons during some heart procedures.

body.heading: What does it check, and how long does it take?
body.body: The British Heart Foundation says an echocardiogram uses sound waves to build up a picture of the heart and its structures, such as the valves. It describes the test as an important investigation for anyone with suspected heart failure, heart valve problems or cardiomyopathy, a disease of the heart muscle. Like other ultrasound scans, which the NHS says do not use radiation, an echocardiogram uses sound waves.

body.heading: Is any preparation needed?
body.body: For a standard echocardiogram people usually need to do nothing to prepare. The exception is the throat version, which may require avoiding eating for several hours.

body.heading: What happens in a standard scan?
body.body: For a standard echocardiogram no preparation is needed, and NHS trust leaflets say people can eat and drink as normal before and afterwards. The person lies on their left side while a cardiac physiologist, a specially trained technician, scans the chest after putting gel on it. The physiologist may ask the person to change position or to hold their breath briefly so that the pictures are clearer. One trust leaflet describes a standard echocardiogram as painless, with no side effects and no radiation.

body.heading: What is a stress echocardiogram like?
body.body: A stress echocardiogram checks how the heart copes with a greater workload, by taking pictures at rest and again under stress. The stress usually comes from walking on a treadmill or, in a dobutamine stress echocardiogram, from a medicine called dobutamine that raises the heart rate. A cardiologist or a specially trained cardiac physiologist supervises the test. Some trust leaflets ask people to avoid certain heart medicines, such as beta blockers, before a dobutamine stress echocardiogram unless the doctor advises otherwise, and each hospital gives its own instructions. Leaflets describe rare complications such as an abnormal heart rhythm and quote different figures, for example around 1 in 1,000 patients in one leaflet and around 1 in 500 in another.

body.heading: How are the results given?
body.body: A cardiac physiologist analyses the recorded images and writes a report for the doctor who requested the test. The doctor who requested the test then receives the report and passes on the results, for example at a clinic appointment or by letter, depending on the trust. One trust leaflet says the letter about stress echocardiogram results, sent to the GP with a copy to the patient, can take about two to four weeks.

references.title: Chelsea and Westminster (NHS trust page): toe

colonoscopy-preparation-and-what-happens.name: Colonoscopy: preparation and what happens
colonoscopy-preparation-and-what-happens.summary: A colonoscopy uses a thin camera to look inside the large bowel. This guide covers bowel preparation, sedation, risks and when results arrive.
keyPoints: A colonoscopy passes a thin, flexible tube with a camera through the bowel to look for the cause of symptoms, to screen for bowel cancer, or to follow up earlier problems.
The bowel must be empty for a clear view, so a bowel preparation, which can include laxatives, is taken beforehand.
Polyps, which are growths on the bowel lining, can be removed during the test and examined under a microscope.
Perforation, a tear in the bowel wall, is the main serious risk and is uncommon, with higher risk when polyps are removed.

body.heading: Why is a colonoscopy done?
body.body: A colonoscopy is often done to look for the cause of bowel symptoms, such as abdominal pain or a change in bowel habit. Colonoscopy is also used to follow up after earlier polyps or bowel cancer, according to MedlinePlus, a US source. People who have had polyps removed before are routinely advised to have repeat colonoscopies.

body.heading: How is the bowel prepared?
body.body: For a clear view, the bowel needs to be empty. Preparation can include laxatives to empty the bowel. Preparation can include clear liquids the day before and laxatives, according to MedlinePlus, a US source. A review of bowel preparation lists vomiting, colicky stomach ache and dizziness among the most common problems. Preparation depends on which type the doctor recommends, and it can differ between hospitals.

body.heading: What happens during the procedure?
body.body: A nurse sees the person first to discuss their medical history, carry out simple checks and explain what will happen. A thin, flexible tube with a camera is passed through the anus and around the large bowel. Air is pumped in to open the bowel, which can cause bloating or cramps. The NHS says a colonoscopy can be uncomfortable but should not be painful. NHS England says a colonoscopy should take 30 to 45 minutes, and a person may be at the hospital for around two hours in total. A leaflet says some people have sedation, some breathe a pain-relieving gas called Entonox, and some have no pain relief. Sedation is given through a thin tube called a cannula in the hand or arm.

body.heading: What are polyps and biopsies?
body.body: Polyps are growths on the bowel lining, and they are usually not cancer. Doctors usually cannot tell the type of polyp just by looking, so suspicious polyps are usually removed and examined under a microscope. Staff can also take small tissue samples, called biopsies, which people typically do not feel. Some findings may be shared once the sedation has worn off, according to MedlinePlus, a US source.

body.heading: What are the risks?
body.body: NHS trust leaflets describe colonoscopy as very safe, with serious complications rare. The main risks are a tear in the bowel wall, called perforation, and bleeding. Trust leaflets give perforation figures that differ, and one says about 1 in 1,000 procedures. The risk rises when polyps are removed, especially large or complex ones. A perforation is treated in hospital, and surgery is sometimes needed, according to NHS trust leaflets. It is common to pass a small amount of blood from the anus after a biopsy or polyp removal. Trust leaflets say a colonoscopy can occasionally miss a problem, including, rarely, a cancer. The NHS says to call NHS 111 or the hospital where the test was done for some symptoms after a colonoscopy, and to call 999 or go to A&E for more serious ones; its page lists which symptoms apply.

body.heading: When do the results come?
body.body: Some NHS trusts say a letter or call with the results comes about two to three weeks after a colonoscopy, though waits can differ. The result will say whether anything abnormal was found and whether further treatment is needed, according to NHS trust pages. If a biopsy was taken, trust leaflets give differing waits for the biopsy results, from several days to several weeks.

references.title: Hull University Teaching Hospitals (NHS trust page): colo
Royal Free London (NHS trust page): colo
Calderdale and Huddersfield (NHS trust page): colo prep

gastroscopy-what-happens-and-what-to-exp.name: Gastroscopy: what happens and what to expect
gastroscopy-what-happens-and-what-to-exp.summary: A gastroscopy uses a thin camera to look at the gullet and stomach. This guide covers fasting, throat spray or sedation, risks and results.
keyPoints: A gastroscopy passes a thin, flexible tube with a camera through the mouth and down to the stomach.
The stomach needs to be empty, and trusts ask for a fast of several hours beforehand.
People can have a throat spray and stay awake, or sedation that leaves them relaxed and drowsy.
Serious complications are rare, but vomiting blood after a gastroscopy is among the reasons the NHS lists for calling 999 or going to A&E.

body.heading: What is a gastroscopy?
body.body: A gastroscopy is a test in which a thin, flexible tube with a small camera goes into the mouth and down into the stomach. The doctor or nurse watches the lining of the gullet, stomach and the first part of the small bowel on a screen. Tiny tissue samples, called biopsies, may be taken, and this is painless.

body.heading: How do people prepare?
body.body: The stomach must be empty, so trusts ask people to stop eating for about six hours beforehand. Many trusts allow sips of clear fluid until about two hours before the test, though some stop earlier.

body.heading: Throat spray or sedation: what is the difference?
body.body: People can usually have a throat spray, sedation, or both, depending on the trust. The throat spray is a local anaesthetic that numbs the back of the throat, and the person stays awake while a nurse talks them through the test. For sedation, a small tube called a cannula is placed in a vein, usually in the back of the hand. The medicine makes the person relaxed and sometimes drowsy, but not fully asleep.

body.heading: What happens during the test?
body.body: Air is passed in to inflate the stomach, which can cause bloating and burping. Trust leaflets give different times for the test itself, and the NHS page gives 15 to 45 minutes. Common effects include a sore throat and bloating, which usually pass within 24 hours, according to trust leaflets.

body.heading: What happens afterwards?
body.body: After a throat spray alone, people may be able to make their own way home, and can drink once swallowing returns to normal, which one leaflet puts at about 20 to 60 minutes. After sedation, people rest in the endoscopy department for an hour or two, according to a trust leaflet. After sedation, an escort is needed to take the person home, and one trust says the sedative can stay in the body for up to 24 hours. One trust says that after sedation, clear thinking and decision-making may be affected for up to 24 hours.

body.heading: What are the risks?
body.body: Serious complications are rare, and trust leaflets give differing figures for a tear in the gut wall, from about 1 in 2,000 to less than 1 in 10,000. Possible problems include a tear in the gut wall that may need surgery, bleeding, and an allergic reaction to the sedation or throat spray. Sedation can occasionally cause short-term problems with breathing, heart rate and blood pressure. Rare complications include damage to loose teeth, crowns or bridgework. The NHS lists vomiting blood after a gastroscopy among the reasons to call 999 or go to A&E.

body.heading: When do the results arrive?
body.body: A doctor or nurse will usually go through the main findings before the person leaves. Biopsy results from the laboratory are not available on the day. Biopsy results go to the referring doctor and the GP, and trust leaflets give waits that range from a couple of weeks to several weeks.

references.title: Leeds Teaching Hospitals (NHS trust page): gastro
University College London Hospitals (NHS trust page): gastro

spirometry-lung-function-test-explained.name: Spirometry: the lung function test explained
spirometry-lung-function-test-explained.summary: Spirometry measures how much air can be blown out and how fast. This guide covers the test, preparation and what results are compared with.
keyPoints: In spirometry the person breathes through a mouthpiece, with a nose clip, into a machine that measures airflow.
Each blow may be repeated several times, with rests in between.
Results are compared with values predicted for someone of the same height, age and sex.
The test may be repeated after a reliever inhaler to see whether it helps breathing.

body.heading: What is spirometry?
body.body: Spirometry is the most common lung function test. It measures how much air a person can blow out and how quickly. Spirometry is the main test for detecting airflow obstruction, while other lung function tests measure lung volumes and gas exchange.

body.heading: What happens during the test?
body.body: The person wears a nose clip so air goes through the mouth, and breathes through a mouthpiece into the lung function machine. They breathe normally, take a deep breath in, and then blow out as hard and fast as possible. Each blow may be repeated several times, with rests in between. One NHS trust says the test normally takes around 15 minutes.

body.heading: Why is spirometry done?
body.body: The NHS says spirometry measures how much air a person can breathe out in one breath, and it is also called a lung function test. It is used to find out whether symptoms come from a lung condition such as asthma, COPD or pulmonary fibrosis (scarring of the lungs), to monitor an existing condition, or to check fitness before surgery. NHS England guidance says NICE recommends quality-assured spirometry as one of several objective tests for diagnosing asthma and COPD. The same guidance says normal spirometry does not rule out asthma.

body.heading: How do people prepare?
body.body: One NHS practice suggests avoiding vigorous exercise for 30 minutes before the test. The same guidance suggests wearing loose clothing. It also notes that a recent chest infection, or recent antibiotics or steroids, can affect the results. Preparation varies, and patients are told whether they need to stop any inhalers or medicines beforehand.

body.heading: How is the test done, according to the NHS?
body.body: NHS trust leaflets say staff record the person's height and weight, which are entered into the machine for the calculations. The person uses a nose clip, breathes in deeply, seals their lips around the tube and breathes out as hard and fast as possible. The NHS says this is repeated two more times, and that staff may ask the person to use an inhaler and repeat the test. The NHS says the appointment should take no more than an hour, and that dizziness during or just after the test is possible but should be brief. The NHS says the test should not be done during a chest infection or soon after a heart attack or stroke. Trust and practice pages say the results are reviewed and then sent to the doctor who requested the test, who discusses them with the person.

body.heading: What is the reliever step?
body.body: The test is sometimes repeated after a reliever inhaler to check whether it helps the airways. The person takes the test, uses the inhaler, waits a short time and repeats the test. The comparison shows how much the airways respond to the medicine, and the test is sometimes used when asthma is being investigated.

body.heading: What do the results show?
body.body: Results are compared with predicted values for someone of the same height, age and sex. A typical report shows the measured values alongside the predicted values. In obstructive conditions such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), the airways narrow, making it harder for air to flow out of the lungs. Restrictive conditions are different, because they decrease the amount of air the lungs can hold. One NHS leaflet says results are discussed at the next clinic appointment with the consultant or GP.

body.heading: Are there any risks?
body.body: NHS leaflets describe the test as painless and non-invasive, with dizziness or fainting the most common side effects and more serious complications very rare. The test needs a good effort, which can make some people feel dizzy or faint. Some people feel dizzy or faint, and coughing is common.

dxa-bone-density-scan-explained.name: DXA bone density scan: what it shows
dxa-bone-density-scan-explained.summary: A DXA scan measures bone density, usually at the hip and spine, using low-dose X-rays. This guide covers who may be referred and what the T-score decides.
keyPoints: A DXA scan is painless: the person lies on a flat table while a scanning arm passes over the hip and lower spine.
The radiation dose is low: the NHS says a DEXA scan uses a much lower level of radiation than a standard X-ray.
The T-score compares bone density with that of a healthy young adult of the same sex.
Treatment decisions use an assessment of the overall chance of breaking a bone, not the scan result alone.

body.heading: What is a DXA scan?
body.body: DXA, also written DEXA, stands for dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, a scan that measures bone density. The scan is used to help diagnose osteoporosis, a condition in which bones become weaker. The NHS describes a DEXA scan as a test that uses low-dose X-rays.

body.heading: Who is offered one?
body.body: NHS trust pages say a doctor can refer a person for a DEXA scan if they may be at risk of osteoporosis, and the criteria differ between services. One NHS trust referral form lists being a current smoker and having had a previous low-trauma fracture among the risk factors it asks about. A doctor usually makes the referral. Results are combined with a fracture risk assessment rather than used alone.

body.heading: Why might a doctor suggest it?
body.body: A bone density scan measures bone density and helps to judge the risk of a fracture. Unlike an ordinary X-ray, it can detect small reductions in bone density, so osteoporosis can be found before a bone breaks. The NHS lists reasons for a scan that include breaking bones easily, long-term use of steroid medicines, and early menopause.

body.heading: What happens during the scan?
body.body: The person lies on their back on a flat table. A scanning arm passes slowly over the body, usually the hip and lower spine. NHS pages describe the scan as quick and painless, and the time it takes varies between services.

body.heading: How much radiation is involved?
body.body: The dose is low. The NHS says a DEXA scan uses a much lower level of radiation than a standard X-ray, similar to what a person is exposed to naturally over about three days.

body.heading: Who should not have one?
body.body: The NHS says the scan uses a low dose of radiation and the risks are much lower than with standard X-rays. Pregnancy is the main caution: the NHS says bone density scans and X-rays are not recommended in pregnancy. The person lies on their back on a flat, open X-ray table while a scanning arm passes slowly over them. An NHS trust page says no special preparation is needed, although metal fasteners on clothing may need to be removed.

body.heading: What do the T-score and Z-score mean?
body.body: The T-score compares a person's bone density with that of a healthy young adult of the same sex. Scores are grouped into bands described as normal, low bone density (osteopenia) and osteoporosis. Osteoporosis is diagnosed using the lowest T-score across the lumbar spine, the neck of the thigh bone and the total hip. The Z-score compares a person with others of the same age, and it is used mainly for premenopausal women, men under 50 and children.

body.heading: Does the result decide treatment?
body.body: A T-score does not decide treatment alone. UK osteoporosis guidance uses a fracture risk tool such as FRAX, which estimates the chance of a broken bone over ten years from bone density and other risk factors, so bone density alone does not decide treatment.

breast-screening-mammogram-what-to-expec.name: Breast screening: who is invited and what happens
breast-screening-mammogram-what-to-expec.summary: NHS breast screening uses mammograms to look for breast cancer in people without symptoms. This guide covers who is invited, the appointment, results and harms.
keyPoints: The NHS offers breast screening from age 50 up to the 71st birthday, with invitations every three years.
A mammogram takes two X-rays of each breast, with each breast pressed between two plates.
Breast screening is offered to people without symptoms to look for breast cancer, and it does not prevent breast cancer.
Screening can miss a cancer and can raise false alarms, and some people are diagnosed with a cancer that would never have caused harm.

body.heading: Who is invited for breast screening?
body.body: The NHS says screening is offered from age 50 up to the 71st birthday. The first invitation usually comes between the ages of 50 and 53, and further invitations follow every three years until the 71st birthday. Anyone registered with a GP as female is invited automatically. People over 71 are not invited automatically but can ask for screening every three years. For trans and non-binary people, eligibility for breast screening depends on the sex registered with the GP and on any hormone treatment or surgery, so NHS guidance advises checking with the GP or local screening service.

body.heading: What happens at the appointment?
body.body: A mammogram takes two X-rays of each breast. Each breast is pressed between two plates, which some people find uncomfortable or painful, but any discomfort should not last long. NHS pages say the mammogram itself takes only a few minutes and the whole appointment should take no longer than 30 minutes.

body.heading: How and when are the results given?
body.body: Results usually come within two weeks of the appointment and are also sent to the GP. If the mammogram needs a closer look, the person is invited back to an assessment clinic for further tests. A Royal Marsden page says about 4 in 100 women are asked to come back, and about three in four of those have normal results after further tests.

body.heading: What are the benefits?
body.body: Breast screening is offered to people without symptoms, using mammograms to look for breast cancer. It does not prevent breast cancer.

body.heading: What are the harms and limits?
body.body: Screening does not always find a cancer that is there, so some people with breast cancer are missed. Some people are asked back for more tests and then found not to have cancer, and the follow-up tests can be invasive and time-consuming. Some people who are screened are diagnosed and treated for a breast cancer that would never have been found or caused them harm.

body.heading: How is it presented as a choice?
body.body: The NHS leaflet 'Helping you decide' describes breast screening as a personal choice and sets out its benefits and risks. It says screening does not prevent breast cancer from developing. Overdiagnosis means finding a cancer that would never have caused harm, and estimates of how often it happens vary between studies. A 2012 independent review estimated that among 10,000 UK women invited to screening from age 50 for 20 years, about 43 breast cancer deaths would be prevented and 129 cancers would be overdiagnosed, although other estimates differ.

body.heading: What if there is a lump between screens?
body.body: Cancer Research UK says anyone who notices changes to their nipples, chest area or armpits should not wait for screening and should tell their doctor.

cervical-screening-what-to-expect.name: Cervical screening: what happens and results
cervical-screening-what-to-expect.summary: Cervical screening checks a sample from the cervix for high-risk HPV. This guide covers who is invited, the appointment and what each result means.
keyPoints: The NHS in England invites people with a cervix aged 25 to 64 for cervical screening.
The sample is tested first for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), the virus that can lead to cell changes.
A negative HPV result means the person is offered screening again in five years.
Cancer Research UK says cervical screening is not a test for cancer; it looks for HPV and cell changes.

body.heading: Who is invited and how often?
body.body: The NHS in England invites people with a cervix aged 25 to 64 for cervical screening. Routine screening is every five years. From 1 July 2025 in England, people who test negative for HPV are offered screening again after five years rather than three; guidance says some people last invited before that date may still be on a three-year interval.

body.heading: What is cervical screening for?
body.body: The NHS describes cervical screening as a test of the health of the cervix that helps to prevent cervical cancer, rather than a test for cancer. The NHS says screening is still important for people who have had the HPV vaccine. Booking is usually through the GP surgery, online or in the NHS App, and some sexual health clinics also offer it.

body.heading: What happens at the appointment?
body.body: Cervical screening is usually done by a female nurse or doctor, and a person can ask for a female practitioner when booking. The clinician gently places a tool called a speculum in the vagina and uses a soft brush to collect cells from the cervix. One source says the test itself should take less than five minutes, and the whole appointment usually lasts 10 to 15 minutes. People can ask for a smaller speculum or ask to insert the speculum themselves. Light spotting for a few hours afterwards is normal.

body.heading: How can the appointment be made easier?
body.body: The NHS suggests wearing something that can stay on during the test, such as a skirt or long top, and bringing someone for support. The NHS says the person can ask to stop at any time and can ask for adjustments, such as a smaller speculum or a different position, to feel more comfortable.

body.heading: Why is the sample tested for HPV?
body.body: Current NHS practice tests the sample for high-risk HPV first. The NHS England guide says high-risk HPV can cause abnormal cell changes that may lead to cervical cancer. If HPV is found, the laboratory then looks more closely at the cells for changes.

body.heading: What do the results mean?
body.body: If HPV is not found, the person is offered screening again in five years. If HPV is found but the cells are normal, the person is usually retested in about 12 months. If HPV is found with abnormal cells, the person is referred for a colposcopy. If more tests are needed, the results letter says what to do next. Results are sent by letter or given by telephone, and the letter says what to do if more tests are needed.

body.heading: What is a colposcopy?
body.body: A colposcopy is the usual next step after an abnormal screening result. Cancer Research UK says cervical screening is not a test for cancer; it looks for HPV and cell changes. A biopsy is examined by a pathologist, who grades any cell changes as CIN1, CIN2 or CIN3.

body.heading: Bleeding or symptoms between screens
body.body: Cancer Research UK advises that bleeding between periods, after sex or after the menopause, or unusual discharge, should be checked by a GP.
